Hello everyone, here is a suggested reading list for those who already consider themselves libertarians but are not sure what to read to further define their beliefs.

Number 10: The privitization of Roads and Highways by Walter Block. http://mises.org/sites/default/files/The%20Privatization%20of%20Roads%20and%20Highways_2.pdf

In this book Walter Block attempts to tackle one of the largest distractions from Anarcho-Capitalist discussions: 'But who will pay for the roads?!' A mix of new material and old articles the book offers consistent libertarian insight into the question at hand. Block systematically tackles the issue of road privatization by addressing how roads would be paid for, who would own them, and debunks the concern that you would be trapped inside your neighborhood dependent on the whims of bi-polar road entrepreneurs. The complexity of the issue is not lost on Block; you will find few 'ceteris paribus' examples in this book and when he begins to discuss coast to coast highways and the property rights associated with sunlight you know the author is not skirting the issue.

Number 9: Nullification -- How to Resist Federal Tyranny in the 21st Century by Thomas E. Woods Jr. http://www.amazon.com/Nullification-Resist-Federal-Tyranny-Century/dp/1596981490

Thomas Woods describes the concept of legal nullification, the method by which laws are not just judged to be broken but whether or not the law itself is just.

Number 8: Hamiltons curse by Robert DiLorenzo: http://www.amazon.com/Hamiltons-Curse-Jeffersons-Revolution-Americans/dp/0307382850

Thomas DiLorenzo is one of two historians I saw speak at CPAC in Washington D.C in early 2010. While most famous (infamous?) for his attacks on Abraham Lincoln this dissection of the havoc wrecked upon America by Alexander Hamilton will have you thanking Aaron Burr every night before you go to bed. This book, in effect, is a history of central banking in the United States. It chronicles the battles fought between Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton stretching from before the revolution to the day Hamilton met his end.

Number 7: The Road to Serfdom Definitive Edition by F.A. Hayek http://mises.org/sites/default/files/Road%20to%20serfdom.pdf

This one is more for the history than the content. You should read it because it is his seminal work that everyone knows, but I didn't particularly like it and from what I understand neither did Hayek.

Number 6: Rollback by Thomas E. Woods Jr. http://www.amazon.com/Rollback-Repealing-Government-Before-Collapse/dp/B005CDT7WM

Whether it is because he is formerly a 'conservative' or simply because he is a very intelligent writer, Dr. Woods does not fall prey to these divisions and Rollback is a great example of this. The book is targeted towards conservative republicans, its recommendations come from members of the Cato institute as well as Fox Business personality Judge Napolitano. A banner on the bottom of the back cover proudly claims 'A MAIN SELECTION OF THE CONSERVATIVE BOOK CLUB'. A passing Democrat would expect this book to be a neo-con dream. Yet Woods is deceptively clever. Rollback starts with examples of how Barack Obama's presidency hurt the American people, luring in the conservatives, then he changes gears and shows how every presidency in the past 50 years has done the same thing, Democrats and Republicans alike.

Number 5: Against Intellectual Property by Stephan Kinsella http://mises.org/sites/default/files/Against%20Intellectual%20Property_2.pdf

Against intellectual Property is by far one of the most important documents in libertarian theory. As far as condensed information goes only Gustav de Molinari's 'The Production of Security' or 'Anatomy of the State' rival 'Against IP'. Kinsella's argument is multi-faceted; he refutes Utilitarian, Natural Rights, Contract and property-rights defenses of IP and the book is targeted towards libertarians and non-libertarians alike. This book is only about 60 pages long but managed to fully convince me that this issue is settled from an An-Cap stand point. Kinsella argues that not only does IP not help innovation but stifles it. The property rights argument was actually settled by Rothbard in Man, Economy, & State where he explicitly proves that recipes are not property and this extends to IP as well being that any given item of IP is not scarce and therefore not an economic good, Kinsella merely elaborates this point but it was a necessary elaboration.

Number 4: Human Action by Ludwig von Mises http://mises.org/sites/default/files/Human%20Action_3.pdf

I like to say that the first 200 pages of this book changed my life, the last 200 changed how I view the world and the middle 400 took me twice as long to read as the other half combined. Political theory mixed with pure economics makes this a vital but sometimes painful read. Do not expect easy prose this time around.

Number 3: Great Wars, Great Leaders by Ralph Raico http://mises.org/sites/default/files/Great%20Wars%20and%20Great%20Leaders%20A%20Libertarian%20Rebuttal_2.pdf

This book could easily have been called 'Churchill: Warmonger and villain'. Raico's dismantling of Churchill extends the figure's entire career and much of his personal life. From his earliest days Churchill longed for power, glory and conflict. He represented the pinnacle of the White Man's Burden and the British Imperialist mindset. Raico uses quotes from personal correspondence as well as official sources to show how Churchill gamed the U.S. into both world wars and how he personally demanded the hunger blockade that killed millions of Germans during the first World War. Truly a damning assembly of facts.

Number 2: Man, Economy and State with Power and Market by Murray Rothbard http://mises.org/sites/default/files/Man%2C%20Economy%2C%20and%20State%2C%20with%20Power%20and%20Market_2.pdf

Anyone who knows much about the late Dr. Rothbard knows that this book started off as merely an elaboration and simplification of Ludwig von Mises' book Human Action. As Rothbard began work examining Mises' theories he began to find flaws and inconsistencies. Rothbard decided that rather than interpret Mises' work for a new generation he would instead improve upon it and make it his own. Nearly 10 years later Rothbard wrote a letter to his teacher and colleague Mises, it simply read 'It is done'.

Man Economy & State is at its heart just like Human Action in it can be used as an economics textbook. The crucial difference however is that ME&S is simply more readable. The prose and wording is much easier to grasp than HA and for obvious reasons; Rothbard wasn't from Austria and was a bit more contemporary. The graphs and statistics are easier to read, the thought process is more transparent and the author's logic is easier to grasp. For these reasons the book is much more useful to those seeking to educate others into the philosophy of liberty.

Number 1: America's Great Depression by Murray Rothbard http://mises.org/rothbard/agd.pdf

America's Great Depression is the most important book for the historical examination of libertarianism. That is no light claim but the content makes it easy to argue. Unlike most books focusing on this time period Roosevelt is barely brought up, instead in true Austrian fashion Rothbard targets the cause of boom that led to the bust and shows how Hoover's actions exacerbated the recession and directly caused the most severe depression of modern times.

By systematically showing the increases in money supply throughout the 1920's as well as the entanglement of the British and American economies Rothbard firmly places the causes of the Great Depression under the auspices of the Austrian Business Cycle Theory. After the description of how and why the inflationary boom of the "roaring" twenties happened(hint: The federal Reserve) Rothbard then goes on to examine nearly every policy action that Hoover took. Most Austro-Libertarians know this already but Hoover was not the free market hero that history has made him out to be, he was in fact the largest source of intervention in the economy up to that point in American history.

To quote Hoover himself in regards to his actions during the depression: "[W]e might have done nothing. That would have been utter ruin. Instead, we met the situation with proposals to private business and to Congress of the most gigantic program of economic defense and counterattack ever evolved in the history of the Republic. We put it into action. No government in Washington has hitherto considered that it held so broad a responsibility for leadership in such times. . . . For the first time in the history of depression, dividends, profits, and the cost of living have been reduced before wages have suffered." If only he realized that falling wages in malinvested areas of production were the cure for depression, not a symptom of it.

Well you did say, "for those who already consider themselves libertarians." I have read America's Great Depression and I agree that it's a great resource for understanding the causes of the Depression. But I think the list may be a bit Austrian-economics-heavy. Libertarians ought to learn at least basic economics (actually, everyone should learn basic economics) but one can be a libertarian without being an economist, and certainly without being an Austrian economist.

It is my belief that a solid foundation in austrian economics opens the door to further libertarian thought. The freedom to engage in trade with others and more importantly why we can own things and ourselves is, in my opinion, a crucial facet of having consistent libertarian ideals. It is the old adage of teaching a man to fish versus giving him a fish. The "why" behind why individual freedom is important is explained through applying austrian economic principles to real situations.

I highly recommend not performing any actions directly on the drive. You can't (easily) control when the OS writes to the disk, so doing a low-level clone (with dd) of the disk to other media should be your first step, then put the source disk away until the recovery is complete. You should end up with a big fat iso (or other raw image) of the disk that you can mount and poke around in.

I did this exact procedure a few months ago and got a complete (partial) recovery just like you want. I need to get a beer to remember how exactly I did it.

DO NOT KEEP TRYING TO DO READ OPERATIONS ON THE DISK ITSELF or you might inadvertently overwrite more data. The dd you did probably pissed on the partition table, among other things.

Edit: Not going to lie, realizing all the stuff I was going to have to type to get out exactly what I did and how it worked...it's just not going to happen. However, I did find this pretty cool article that mentions moe's testdisk, as well as ddrescue and PhotoRec. I think these tools will probably get you what you need without you needing to understand how hard drives and filesystems work underneath. Good luck.
